lead: A GIS layer is only as good as the data pushed into it. Data input turns a paper toposheet, a total station file, a satellite image or a spreadsheet into points, lines and polygons in the chosen model. Editing then removes the geometric and attribute errors that digitising always creates. Verification proves the layer against independent evidence — control-point residuals and a field sample — before any analysis is trusted. Real projects spend more time here than on analysis: a city corporation digitising property boundaries, or a highway authority importing total station files, will both live with these errors for years.
prereq: You need: 7.3 for the two data models and 7.2 for spatial versus attribute data; see Unit 1 for map scales and sheet numbering, and Unit 5 for total station and GNSS capture.

blocks.text: Every layer starts as something else: a paper toposheet, a total station or GNSS file, a satellite image, a scanned revenue record, a spreadsheet, or crowd-picked points. None of these is a clean layer. Input is the work of converting each source into features with coordinates and attributes.

items: Manual digitising: the sheet is fixed on a digitising table and the cursor is traced along each feature; the table sends coordinates to the software.
On-screen (heads-up) digitising: a scanned or georeferenced image sits behind the cursor and you click each vertex.
Scanning and vectorising: software thins scanned lines to centrelines, then you correct the result.
COGO entry: bearings, distances and offsets from survey records are typed in, and the software computes coordinates.
Direct import: total station and GNSS files carry point number, easting, northing, elevation and a feature code.
Image interpretation: features are identified and traced on a rectified image (see Unit 6).

blocks.text: A scanned sheet has pixel coordinates, not ground coordinates. Georeferencing fixes that. Pick control points whose ground coordinates are known — grid intersections on a toposheet, or points surveyed with GNSS. Fit a transformation from pixel position to easting and northing: four points allow an affine fit, six or more allow a second-order fit that absorbs scanner distortion. At each control point compare the transformed position with the known position; the difference is the residual, in metres, split into easting and northing.

blocks.where: eᵢ, nᵢ are the easting and northing residuals at control point i, in metres; n is the number of control points; RMS is the combined root-mean-square error in metres. It equals √(s²ₑ + s²ₙ), where s²ₑ = Σeᵢ²/n and s²ₙ = Σnᵢ²/n are the mean squared residuals in each axis.

blocks.text: Compare the RMS with the tolerance the scale allows. A 1:50 000 toposheet supports about 12.5 m on the ground (0.25 mm at map scale × 50 000). If RMS exceeds tolerance, improve or re-survey the control and refit — do not simply accept the picture.
Switch on snapping before digitising, not after. Within the snap tolerance a new vertex takes an existing node's coordinate exactly, so two lines share one point instead of two points a hair apart.

items: Add or delete vertices to reshape a line.
Split a line where the feature changes; merge two lines that are the same road or boundary.
Trim overshoots, lines that run past the line they should touch, and extend undershoots, which stop short.
Close polygons that fail to close on their last vertex.
Delete duplicate nodes: two vertices at one coordinate.

Remove slivers: thin polygons formed when two boundaries that should coincide are digitised a few metres apart. A sliver has no real owner; left in place it steals area from one side and adds it to the other.

blocks.text: Topology is the stored record of which lines meet, which lines bound which polygon, and which polygons are adjacent. Build it, then test it. This finds what a tidy screen hides: dangles (an endpoint touching nothing), unclosed polygons, and crossings with no node. Repair, then rebuild before attributes go in.

Each attribute field has a type — integer, real, text or date — and a domain, the allowed values such as a fixed land-use code list. Each record needs a unique key so the feature and its record join one to one (see 7.2). Duplicate records break every count and every area total.
Verification asks whether the layer matches the ground, not whether it looks neat. Five checks cover it.

items: Positional accuracy: control-point residuals, plus independently surveyed check points not used in the fit.
Attribute accuracy: field-sample the parcels. 46 correct out of 50 sampled gives 92 %; always report the sample size.
Logical consistency: no dangles, no unclosed polygons, no polygon with two owners, no negative length.
Completeness: every source feature is present; count features per sheet against the source.
Edge matching: a road crossing a sheet boundary must have identical coordinates on both sheets. If it stops 30 m short of its neighbour, the join is wrong.

blocks.text: Metadata records source, date, scale, datum, projection, units, transformations applied, RMS and known gaps. Without it no later user can judge the layer (see 7.5).

Manipulation reshapes the layer for use: transformation (reprojection), rubber sheeting (warping a layer to fit control points), edge matching, clipping to a boundary, format conversion between shapefile, GeoJSON and GeoPackage, and merging adjacent sheets. Record each operation and verify the layer again afterwards; overlay analysis is covered in 7.6.

examples.question: A 1:50 000 toposheet is georeferenced on four control points. The residuals, written as (easting, northing) in metres, are: P1 (+2.0, +1.0), P2 (−1.0, +2.0), P3 (+1.0, −2.0), P4 (−2.0, −1.0). The project tolerance is 5 m. (a) Compute the RMS error. (b) State whether the layer is accepted. (c) Cleaning finds 7 dangles, 3 slivers and 2 duplicate nodes. State the repair order before attribute entry and why.
steps: Square the easting residuals: 2.0² = 4.0, (−1.0)² = 1.0, 1.0² = 1.0, (−2.0)² = 4.0. Sum = 10.0 m².
Square the northing residuals: 1.0² = 1.0, 2.0² = 4.0, (−2.0)² = 4.0, (−1.0)² = 1.0. Sum = 10.0 m², so s²ₙ = 10.0 ÷ 4 = 2.5 m².
2.24 m is below the 5 m tolerance, and also below the 12.5 m the 1:50 000 scale allows, so the layer is accepted.

Repair order: delete the 2 duplicate nodes first, then fix the 7 dangles by extending undershoots and trimming overshoots, then delete the 3 slivers and rebuild topology. A sliver has no real owner, so attributes attached to it before repair would be counted twice or lost.
examples.answer: RMS error = 2.24 m, below the 5 m tolerance, so the layer is accepted; the 2 duplicate nodes, 7 dangles and 3 slivers are repaired and topology rebuilt before attributes are entered.
examples.check:
import math
e = [2.0, -1.0, 1.0, -2.0]
n = [1.0, 2.0, -2.0, -1.0]
sse = sum(x*x for x in e)
ssn = sum(y*y for y in n)
mse_e = sse/len(e)
mse_n = ssn/len(n)
rms = math.sqrt(mse_e + mse_n)
print(round(mse_e, 4))
print(round(mse_n, 4))
print(round(rms, 4))

traps: Judging quality by how tidy the screen looks. Dangles, slivers and duplicate nodes look harmless and still break area and overlay results.
Mixing digitising precision with positional accuracy: storing coordinates to four decimals does not move the point closer to the ground.
Quoting attribute accuracy without the sample size, or sampling only the parcels you already believe are correct.
Editing a layer but forgetting to rebuild topology, so adjacency and polygon areas stay stale.
Accepting a georeference on RMS alone when one corner has a 15 m residual — look at the residuals point by point.

quiz.a: Georeferencing fits a transformation from image or pixel coordinates to ground coordinates using control points of known position. The residual is the difference, in metres easting and northing, between a control point's transformed position and its known position.

quiz.q: What is a sliver and why is it removed?
quiz.a: A thin polygon formed when two boundaries that should coincide are digitised a few metres apart. It is removed because it has no real owner and wrongly takes area from one polygon and adds it to the other.

quiz.q: Why should snapping be on during digitising rather than used only afterwards?
quiz.a: Snapping during digitising makes shared vertices identical as they are created; afterwards the two lines already have separate coordinates and each gap or overlap must be found and repaired by hand. Prevention is cheaper than repair.

quiz.q: Distinguish a dangle from an undershoot.
quiz.a: A dangle is an endpoint that touches no other line at all. An undershoot is a line that was meant to reach another line but stops a short distance before it, leaving a gap that breaks the polygon.

quiz.q: Residuals at three control points are (+1.0, 0.0), (0.0, +2.0), (−1.0, 0.0) metres. Compute the RMS error.
50 parcels are field-checked against the attribute table; 46 are correct. State the attribute accuracy as a sentence for a report.
quiz.a: Attribute accuracy is 46 ÷ 50 × 100 = 92 %, estimated from a field sample of 50 parcels.

quiz.q: A merged two-sheet layer passes the RMS test but fails edge matching along the shared boundary. Give two likely causes and the checks you would make.
quiz.a: Likely causes: the two sheets were georeferenced with different control points or a different datum and projection, or the shared boundary was digitised twice, once on each sheet. Checks: compare the datum, projection and units in both metadata records, inspect residuals near the boundary, then refit both sheets to common control points and edge-match the boundary line so the coordinates are identical.

beyond: Not for the exam. In practice this work now lives inside spatial databases, where topology rules reject a bad polygon at the moment of insert rather than in a later cleaning pass. Open standards for simple features decide how geometry and attributes travel between systems, so validation rules are increasingly written once and reused. Land-record modernisation programmes in India rise or fall on exactly this step, because a boundary digitised twice produces disputes that no analysis can settle. Search next for topology rules in GIS, positional accuracy standards for spatial data, and the validation functions of PostGIS.
